questions.question: Does technical SEO matter at all if my content is thin?
questions.answer_summary: Technical SEO is necessary but not sufficient — pages need to be crawlable/indexable to have any chance of ranking, but technical fixes alone won't make thin content rank.

questions.question: What counts as 'thin content' in Google's eyes?
questions.answer_summary: Thin content includes pages with little substance (e.g., ~200-word articles), doorway pages, programmatically generated pages, and low-value heavily promotional/affiliate content.

questions.question: Can thin content actually trigger a penalty?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — thin content is explicitly named as a violation of Google's spam policies and can lead to ranking penalties.

questions.question: Does Google evaluate quality page-by-page or across the whole site?
questions.answer_summary: John Mueller has stated that Google's quality algorithms look at the website overall — 'they look at everything that's indexed' — not just the individual page being evaluated.

questions.question: Can a small amount of fluff content drag down an otherwise good site?
questions.answer_summary: Mueller has warned that low-quality 'fluff' content (he's referred to some SEO content as 'digital mulch') can cause Google's systems to assume the entire site has mediocre content.

questions.question: If I fix all my technical SEO issues, will my thin content start ranking?
questions.answer_summary: No — recovery examples typically involve fixing technical issues, removing/improving low-quality content, and adding genuinely higher-quality content together, not technical fixes in isolation.

questions.question: Is 'content is king' actually good advice, or an oversimplification?
questions.answer_summary: An industry piece titled 'Content Is King: The Greatest Lie Ever Told In SEO' argues content alone is only one piece of the puzzle — without indexing, link signals, and freshness, even great content stays invisible.

questions.question: In what order should a small business fix technical SEO vs. content?
questions.answer_summary: A commonly suggested sequence for SMEs is baseline technical cleanup first, then focused content expansion, with technical maintenance ongoing in the background — rather than treating either as a one-time fix-it-and-forget step.

questions.question: Can fixing crawl/indexing/speed issues ever move rankings more than adding content?
questions.answer_summary: A Hacker News discussion specifically framed as 'technical SEO vs. content optimization: which one moves rankings?' found that in some cases, fixing crawl, indexing, or performance issues had a bigger measured impact than publishing more content.

questions.question: What's actually included under 'technical SEO'?
questions.answer_summary: Technical SEO covers crawlability, indexation, site architecture, page speed, mobile usability, structured data, canonicalization, and internal linking logic — the infrastructure layer that makes content discoverable.

questions.question: Will a technically flawless site with thin service pages actually compete for real queries?
questions.answer_summary: No — the consensus framing is that a technically clean site with thin service pages 'will not compete for meaningful queries,' just as a content-heavy site with indexation problems wastes its own content investment.

questions.question: Does removing thin content ever help more than adding new content?
questions.answer_summary: Yes in some documented recovery cases — sites combined removing/improving existing thin content with technical fixes rather than only adding more new pages.
